lessons.title: Being a good worker and team member
lessons.html:
Skills for the workplace

Being good at your job is not only about using a knife well. It is also about how you work with others, how you communicate, and how you look after yourself. These skills help you keep your job, earn the trust of your supervisor and grow in your career.

Work ethic

  • Be on time: the slaughter line cannot start if people are missing. If you will be late or absent, phone your supervisor before the shift starts.
  • Be reliable: do your job properly every time, even when no one is watching.
  • Follow instructions and procedures, especially on hygiene and safety.
  • Be honest: report mistakes and problems. Hiding a mistake, such as a dropped carcass, can make people ill.
  • Respect your colleagues, supervisors and inspectors, whatever their language, culture or gender.

Teamwork on the line

On a slaughter line, each person does one step. If one person works too slowly or badly, everyone after them is affected. Help new workers, share knowledge, and speak up politely when you see a problem.

Communication

  • Listen carefully to instructions. If you do not understand, ask again. It is better to ask than to guess.
  • Speak clearly and politely. In a noisy plant, use agreed hand signals.
  • When you report something, say what happened, where and when.
  • Read the notices, signs and work instructions in your area.

Handling conflict

Disagreements happen. Stay calm, do not shout or fight, and talk to the person privately. If that does not solve it, ask your supervisor to help, or use the grievance procedure. Violence at work leads to dismissal.

lessons.title: Rights, money, health and growing your career
lessons.html:
Know your rights and duties

  • You should have a written contract with your job, hours, wage and leave.
  • The Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 covers working hours, overtime, leave and payslips. The National Minimum Wage Act sets the lowest wage that may be paid.
  • The OHS Act 85 of 1993 gives you the right to a safe workplace and the duty to work safely.
  • COIDA covers you if you are injured at work. UIF helps if you lose your job.
  • You have the right to join a trade union.

Managing your money

Check your payslip every pay day: hours, rate, overtime and deductions (UIF, tax, union fees, loans). Ask the office if something is wrong.

  • Make a simple budget: write down your income, then your fixed costs (rent, transport, food, school fees), then savings.
  • Save a little every month, even R50, for emergencies.
  • Be careful of loan sharks (mashonisas) and lenders who keep your bank card. Use only registered credit providers and only borrow what you can pay back.

Basic numeracy at work

You will use numbers every day: carcass numbers, mass in kilograms, temperatures, counting animals and reading the time sheet. For example, if 120 cattle must be slaughtered and the line does 15 per hour, it will take 120 ÷ 15 = 8 hours.

Health and wellness

  • Eat well, drink water and sleep enough; slaughter work is physically demanding.
  • Avoid alcohol and drugs; they cause accidents.
  • Know your HIV status and protect yourself. Use the wellness programme or the clinic.
  • Ask for help with stress; many workplaces have an employee assistance programme.

Growing your career

Learn more than one job on the line. Keep your training certificates. With experience and further qualifications you can become a team leader, a supervisor or a quality controller.

Key points

  • Be on time, reliable, honest and respectful.
  • Listen, ask when unsure, and report clearly what, where and when.
  • Know your rights under labour and safety laws.
  • Check your payslip, budget and avoid loan sharks.
  • Look after your health and keep learning to grow your career.
